title: The $15 billion ad-powered AI startup your doctor may already be using
gist: OpenEvidence, an ad-supported medical AI search engine used by nearly two-thirds of US doctors, raised $250 million at a $15 billion valuation and is on track for $400-500 million in 2026 ad revenue, while facing competition from OpenAI and Anthropic, mixed accuracy evidence and an EU/UK withdrawal.

insights.claim: Nearly two-thirds of US doctors use OpenEvidence's AI search, which processed more than 42 million prompts last month, and the company has a $15 billion valuation after a $250 million round in September.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Physician workflow penetration is the moat for an ad-supported healthcare AI model.

insights.claim: OpenEvidence has drawn nearly $1 billion in 18 months from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Blackstone, Thrive Capital and Sequoia.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Top-tier capital is underwriting vertical AI with consumer-style virality.

insights.claim: OpenEvidence booked $100 million in ad buys for the year by end-2025 and is on track for $400 million to $500 million in ad revenue by end of 2026, according to a person close to the company.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Pharma and healthcare advertising is a large pool monetizing physician attention.

insights.claim: Nadler calls OpenEvidence the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare, growing largely by word of mouth in a sector where few tools have seen similar traction.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Bottom-up physician adoption bypasses slow enterprise sales cycles.
insights.quote: We’re the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare
insights.locator: The ads-powered platform has grown largely

insights.claim: Wolters Kluwer released an AI version of its UpToDate tool in October 2025, nearly two years after OpenEvidence entered the market, showing incumbents were sluggish to adopt generative AI.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Incumbent medical-reference vendors face displacement risk.
insights.locator: Nadler’s company has penetrated an established market

insights.claim: OpenAI with ChatGPT for healthcare and Anthropic with healthcare tools are pushing into the space, though Anthropic recently partnered with OpenEvidence to bring tools to 100 low- and middle-income countries.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Frontier labs are a nascent threat but also partners.
insights.locator: The company needs to see off competition

insights.claim: Mount Sinai, Memorial Sloan Kettering and NYU Langone have integrated or formalized ties with OpenEvidence, embedding it in electronic health records after clinicians were already using it as an independent resource.
insights.speaker: Financial Times

insights.claim: Nadler said the end game is literature-based drug discovery, whose economic value he expects to dwarf by orders of magnitude what the company could charge hospitals or advertisers, with clinical trials launching in coming weeks.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Strategic pivot from ad-supported search to pharma R&D is the real valuation bet.
insights.quote: The end game is literature-based drug discovery
insights.locator: Nadler said it will also launch clinical trials

insights.claim: OpenEvidence withdrew from the EU and UK earlier this year over the bloc's AI Act, stymieing expansion into two key markets.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: AI Act compliance cost can push US AI products out of European markets.

insights.claim: A Mayo Clinic study found OpenEvidence gave accurate, evidence-based recommendations in all five sampled patient cases though its impact on treatment decisions was limited, but a June Nature paper found it underperformed general-purpose models such as Gemini and GPT on clinical benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Mixed evidence challenges the premise that a narrow source list beats frontier models.

insights.claim: Neurosurgeon Eric Oermann said there is a lack of research on individual AI tools' performance and scant guidance on clinical implementation, and there are concerns junior doctors may over-rely on these tools before mastering basics.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Liability and clinical-safety scrutiny is a risk to adoption.
insights.locator: Eric Oermann, a neurosurgeon at NYU Langone
